Sir,

I have the honour to report that Mr. L.E.
de S. Hoover, the American citizen about whom
there has been considerable correspondence
concerning arms smuggling, was seen in the
American Club at 12 noon on March 26 wearing
a Police armlet and lanyard with pistol
attached. Mr. Hoover is not a member of the
Police Specials or the S.V.C.

I have the honour to be,
Sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sd) E.J.M. Barrett.

Sir,
With reference to attached "Confidential" letter,
Lawerence E. de S. Hoover is living at present in an apartment
with Paul Stanley Ericson (Italian) at the "Blackstone Apartment
Building", Rue Lafayette, Frenchtown. They removed there on
August 1, 1926, from their rooms at the A.P.C. Building, 7th
floor, 1 The Bund.
In May 1926 Hoover approached Mr. E.H. Staber,
Operating Department Manager of the Standard Oil Company, 11/12
Canton Road, re sale of Thompson Sub Machine Guns for the
Company's up river steam boats. At the time Hoover stated it was
necessary for the Company to make application for a "Huchow"
through their Consul (American) before they would be allowed to
import such guns into China. This was done, but the American
Minister McMurray at Pekin could not see his way to make
application for this special permit to the Chinese Government
to import such class of guns as it was not consistent with the

ammunition for same, therefore the deal automatically dropped.
As regards the remark about getting the guns, etc. via Germany,
that was only in casual conversation with reference to possibili-
ties of bringing such a type of defence to China without a "Huchow".

COPY of Police Report dated August 13, 1926

Lawrence E. de S. Hoover is living at present in an
apartment with Paul Stanley Ericson(Italian) at the "Blackstone
Apartment Building", Rue Lafayette.

In May 1926 Hoover approached Mr. E.H. Staber,
Operating Department Manager of the Standard Oil Company, 11/12
Canton Road, re sale of Thompson Sub Machine Guns for the
Company's up river steam boats. At the time Hoover stated it
was necessary for the Company to make application for a "Huchow"
through their Consul before they would be allowed to import
such guns into China. This was done, but the American Minister
could not see his way to make application for this special per-
mit to the Chinese Government to import such class of guns as
it was not consistent with the "Importation of Arms for Foreigners
"Arms Regulations promulgated at Peking in 1908".

Hoover since selling the 16 Sub Machine Guns to the
S.M.P. has brought himself into prominence before the various
classes of Foreigners in Shanghai. He has always, since coming
to Shanghai over a year ago, stated he was the Far East Represen-
tative for the Auto-Ordnance Corporation of New York, and what
apparently has caused suspicious comment against him is the
manner in which he runs around Shanghai and always has money
behind him despite the fact that the sale of machine guns to the
S.M.P. is the only transaction he has made on behalf of his
employers. It is said, however, that he has a private income
which makes him independent of the position he holds with the
Auto-Ordnance Corporation.

- 2 -

On July 6,1926, a Municipal Police representative had
a conversation with him regarding Thompson Sub Machine Guns and
the methods of smuggling same into China. He was unaware that
information regarding his knowledge on this question was being
sought. He was very frank and stated that in America it is un-
necessary to have a license to buy and sell guns of such type,
and they were sold in U.S.A. at $175, but for export purposes
a State license would have to be granted. However, employees
aboard steam boats plying between China and America smuggled
those arms into the former country and through secret sources
managed to get them through to Chinese Warlords such as Chang
Tso Lin, etc. and quite easily sell same for prices ranging
from $1,000 to $1,200. The Auto-Ordnance Corporation,however,
would not export the Sub Machine Gun except through official
channels. On being asked if it was possible t o bring such guns
through Germany, he admitted they could be shipped from U.S.A.
to Hamburg, but did not proceed to state how or what route they
would take from there to China. He admitted he knew gun-runners
in Shanghai,but their principles in transactions were such that
they did not touch any of the arms sold, and therefore no action
could be taken against them owing to their intricate methods.
It has been learned confidentially that the local office
of the Canadian Pacific Steamships Ltd., were requested by the
Hongkong Office about October 1925 to make enquiries re Hoover.
So far nothing tangible has been discovered to prove that
Hoover is gun running.

Memorandum.

Shanghai, 16 6 1926.

To Dep Inspector

It is reliably reported that Mr Hoover, who sold
Riot Guns to the Council, tried to sell further guns to
the Standard Oil Co for use on boats upriver and stated
that there would be no difficulty in getting these guns, etc into
China via Germany in spite of the Custom Regulations. I
suggest his movements might be watched as he is quite
probably prepared to sell these guns to any one willing to
pay for them. The Standard Oil Co turned the offer
down. The information comes from Mr Perry (of the Standard
Oil Co) via Sanborn & Highland.

S.C.
For confidential enquiries
It is more than likely.

THE COMPANY TO WHICH HOOVER WAS ACCREDITED
NAMELY THE AUTO ORDNANCE CORPORATION HAVE REPEATEDLY
CABLED HIM TO RETURN TO NEW YORK CITY. THEY HAVE
RECEIVED NO ANSWER FROM HIM. NOTHING IN A COMMERCIAL
WAY HAS COME FROM HIS ACTIVITY IN SHANGHAI. THE
COMPANY APPEARS ANXIOUS TO ASCERTAIN WHAT THIS MAN
IS DOING.

Copy of Letter dated July 14th, 1926, sent to Felix
Simonpietri, Commander Supply Corp, U. S. Navy.
------------------

My dear Commander,

L. E. de S. Hoover arrived in Shanghai
just over a year ago and stated that he was the Far East
Representative for the Auto-Ordnance Coy of New York.
He received an order from the Council for 16 guns and
some spare parts. These were subsequently delivered.
He then appointed Frank Chamberlin as agent here, but
a week or so later cancelled this appointment. Chamberlin,
who had got two extra guns, refused to return them unless
given a commission on the sixteen which he (Chamberlin)
had been largely instrumental in persuading the Council
to purchase. Subsequently Chamberlin wrote to me from
New York saying that he had visited the Auto-Ordnance
people and had found that Hoover was a salesman pure
and simply, and had no authority to appoint agents, and
had, in fact, outstayed his time in China very considerably
and would not receive his expenses. Various other
persons in Shanghai also apparently view Hoover with
suspicion, and enquiries were made some time ago by the
U.S. Consul-General regarding his bona - fide. During
the year he has paid visits to Manila, Tientsin, Peking, Mukden
and Japan. So far as I can gather the only business he has
put through is the sale of 16 sub-machine guns to the S.M.
Police. He has paid one or two visits to Chinese officials
in the native city, his excuse being that it was in order to
find out whether any guns were leaking into Chapei, etc.
The foregoing are the reasons for suspecting his bona-fides,
but there is nothing very definite to go upon, and Chamberlin's

- 2 -

story of his call on the Company is possibly biassed.
    In order, however, to settle the question once
and for all, it would greatly assist us if you could
ascertain from New York or Washington whether he has
full powers as a representative of the Auto-Ordnance
Corporation - and if so why he should have remained
here for so long without apparently doing any business ?

        Yours very sincerely,

        (Sd)    W. Beatty.

N.C.D.N. 16-6-26.

Arms for China

Louis Joseph Levy, a Victoria
merchant, has been found guilty at
the Victoria, B. C., Assizes of smugg-
ling machine guns into Canada from
the United States. They were des-
tined for China, presumably for one
of the warring factions. Thomas
Ling Newton, similarly charged,
was acquitted. Argument as to
whether Levy is guilty in law as
well as in fact is proceeding. In
this, Levy's counsel in putting up a
strong fight. The indictment said
the goods were smuggled into
Canada. The evidence went to
show that Vancouver was the port
of entry and he claimed that the
onus was on the Crown to show
that the guns, prohibited articles,
had been imported without the con-
sent of the Minister of Customs. In
court, five Thompson sub-machine
guns, a weapon resembling a large
revolver, on a shortened army rifle
tripod, four drums of one hundred
cartridges and several smaller
drums were displayed. The arrest
of Levy and his companion, Newton,
was dramatic. The accused was
watched all the way from Vancouver
to Victoria by customs officers who
went on the steamer. Levy checked
out his two suitcases, called a taxi,
picked up the trunks and put them
in a taxi. He pulled down the
blinds and as he did so handed
something to the steward. Two
customs officers "sprang" from no-
where, jumped on the running board
and ordered the driver to drive to
the customs house. The munitions
were then discovered.

Made by D. I. Sullivan. Forwarded by W. Givens C. S. I.

Sir,
The attached telegram was shown to Mr. Hamilton,
United States Consul, on March 22. After consulting the
United States Consul General, Mr. Hamilton, said that the
Consular Authorities believe Hoover is the representative of
the Auto-Ordnance Corporation of New York. He added that
the Consul General had taken a copy of the telegram and
requested that in case any business is done in the matter
the United States Consulate either in Shanghai or Hankow
be informed. Mr. Hamilton added that the Consul-General
thanked the Police for showing him the telegram, and for
the confidential information of the Police said that they
are keeping Hoover under surveillance.

I am, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
J. Sullivan.

December 28, 1925.

Commissioner of Police,

Mr. L.E. Hoover came to Shanghai as an
accredited representative of the Auto-Ordnance
Corporation of New York. The sixteen Thompson
Sub-Machine Guns now in the possession of the S.M.P.
were purchased through him.

At the time when the order was being placed
I suggested that we would like to see the Thompson
Auto-Rifle, which he had stated to be a very distinct
improvement on the modern army rifle. The rifle
in question was accordingly shipped to Shanghai by
the "President Jackson", but was apparently mislaid
in transit, being subsequently returned to Mr. Hoover
from Hongkong.

I understand that Mr. Hoover left on December 26,
1925 for Peking, taking with him the bolt of the Auto-
Rifle. The rifle (minus bolt) is now in my office,
boxed-up, and addressed "L.E. Hoover, International
Banking Corporation, Yokohama", also 500 rounds .30
Springfield ammunition.

AUTO-ORDNANCE CORPORATION.
302 Broadway.
New York City.

November 17, 1925.

Mr. L.E. Hoover,
c/o International Banking Corporation,
Shanghai, China.

Dear Mr. Hoover:

We enclose herewith B/L and memorandum invoice cover-
ing the autorifle and 500 cal. .30 cartridges, which went forward to
you November 10th via the Steamer President Jackson. On the same
vessel was the shipment for the Municipal Council; copy of invoice
and packing list are also attached.

The numerous delays in connection with the making of
this shipment have been almost heartbreaking. When we received your
first cable regarding the order of the Council on September 29th we
practically moved heaven and earth to get the license from the State
Department and the goods to Vancouver to go on the Empress of Russia.
The license was received from the State Department and the shipment
was at Vancouver on time but at the last moment the Canadian Pacific
officials refused to accept the permit of our State Department. Ar-
rangements were then made to forward the goods on the President Grant
from Seattle. From the constant communications we had with our ex-
port broker we understood that the Canadian Pacific people reversed
themselves and agreed to ship on the Empress of Australia and we
thought the goods were well on their way to Shanghai when we received
word that the shipment had not gone forward. Copy of letter from
our forwarding agents, the Independent Forwarding Company, setting
forth some of the difficulties in making this shipment is attached.

Now the consignment for the Council did not include
the spare parts enumerated in their letter of September
29th as we did not know spare parts were required until we received
the letter, which, of course, was subsequent to your cable. However,
these spare parts are now on the Coast awaiting shipment and will go
forward on the next steamer together with a mount. License has been
procured. In connection with the mounts, Colonel Thompson instructs
us to inform you that the guns do not need studs. They fit in the
mount and the Indian people have informed us that they have put in
their machines the base into which the mount will fit. We might say
here with reference to your complaint as to our quotation on the
Indian motorcycles that it was based on the quotation of the Indian
people to us and no effort was made to make any profit whatsoever.
We simply added $125.00 to cover the cost of the mount to their
quotation. The mount we are having made up to replace the one sent
the Council is costing us $175.00. It is understood, of course,
that the Indian people did not make much of a concession to us,
and that is to be expected since they naturally did not want us
to be bidding against their dealers. While they may not have had
any dealer in Shanghai they did not know that the machines were
intended for that place. We did not so inform them at the time
although as their Export Manager, Mr. McGann, informed us they
so understood from the quantity desired.

(2)

We have sent B/L, insurance certificates and
invoice to the Shanghai Municipal Council through the bank
together with sight draft for $5,667.61 per instructions contained
in letter of September 29th.

We are all elated at this first business from
China and are confidently awaiting further developments. Next
time we promise you the shipments will be made with greater
facility. We won't waste any time on the Canadian Pacific.

Yours very truly,

(sd) T.A. Clarke,
Secretary,
Auto-Ordnance Corporation.

TAC'L
Encls.

November 10, 1925.

Auto-Ordnance Corporation,
302 Broadway,
New York City.

Gentlemen:

We refer to the shipments which you requested us to con-
sign to the Canadian Pacific Railway at Vancouver, for the Shanghai
Municipal Council, covering 10 cases, and to L.E. Hoover, 2 cases.

We regret to say that we have experienced very unpleasant
and dissatisfactory relations in the manner which the Canadian Pacific
Railway have handed these matters. For your enlightment and inform-
ation, we feel that we must express some of the difficulties with
these people.

On October 8th, we advised Mr. J.C. McNab, the Foreign
Freight Agent at Vancouver, of the Canadian Pacific Railway, that the
shipments were going to go forward, and thereby enclosed the Depart-
ment of State license No. 197 and 199.

On October 16th, an elapse of 9 days, the Canadian Pacific Railway
of New York office, telephoned us that they regret the shipment not
being able to go on board the Empress of Russia, owing to some
customs formalities which did not permit the Canadian Government
release, and they informed us that they would have this shipment go forward
on the S.S. President Grant (Admiral Oriental Line), sailing on the
8th of October. We advised them that since it did not go forward on
the Empress of Russia, we were particularly anxious that it go forward
on the next boat, and instructed them to have it go forward on the
President Grant rather than hold the shipment for a period of 2 weeks
more or less. On October 28th, the New York office of the Canadian
Pacific Railway advised us that the Admiral Oriental Line insisted upon
a guarantee to pay any additional charges in the event this consignment
was to be returned, and after some numerous discussion, that we though
they handled this matter in the most indiscreet manner, giving us last
minutes advices. We finally consented to give them a guarantee for
this request, and also expected that this shipment would go forward on
the President Grant. We wired the Admiral Oriental Line to ascertain
if same went forward on the President Madison, but with no response,
and telephoned the Canadian Pacific Railway again, their Mr. Morton,
who advised, on the morning of November 7th, that he was just in receipt
of a telegram that a discrepancy in the mark was found, and that one
case of clips was marked ALC, instead of one case safety metallic
cartridges for L.E. Hoover marked L.E.H. We immediately telegraphed
the Admiral Oriental Line to advise us the name of shipper and the
contents of this particular case and learned that they did not receive
necessary instructions from the Canadian Pacific Railway of Vancouver,
regarding the shipment, and requested us by telegraph to favor them with
the name of the consignees and the number of packages to be shipped to
each, whether the freight was to be prepaid or collect, and the number
of ladings to be issued.

(2)

We feel that a great injustice was done to both your office
and ourselves, by the Canadian Pacific Railway, in not complying with
the original instructions, and then again in not conveying the necessary
instructions to the Admiral Oriental Line for the immediate trans-
shipment of this consignment.

In conclusion, we have again telegraphed the Admiral Oriental
Line at Seattle, giving them final instructions regarding this shipment
and to hold the one box which they claimed contained clips marked:
AIC, to open the case and advise us of the contents. We await tele-
graph advice most any moment from Seattle, as to the status of this con-
signment. In view of the foregoing, we trust you can readily appre-
ciate the fact that we have exercised all care for the dispatch of
these goods, and must enlighten you that if you intend to have further
shipments to Shanghai, it would be most advisable to have same in care
of our agent in Seattle, where individual attention may be prevalent
as we have served you in the past for five years in New York.

For your information, we have numerous other communications
between the office of the Canadian Pacific Railway at Vancouver, and
the Deputy Minister of Customs at Ottawa, Canada, and should you wish
to peruse our papers in connection with this matter if necessary, we
shall be pleased to submit same to you.

As soon as we hear from the Admiral Oriental Line we shall
not fail to advise you by telephone as promptly as possible.

Very truly yours,

INDEPENDENT FORWARDING CO., INC.
(sd) H.S. Dorf.

We feel that a great injustice was done to both your office 
and ourselves, by the Canadian Pacific Railway, in not complying with 
the original instructions, and then again in not conveying the necessary 
instructions to the Admiral Oriental Line for the immediate trans- 
shipment of this consignment. 


In conclusion, we have again telegraphed the Admiral Oriental 
Line at Seattle, giving them final instructions regarding this shipment 
and to hold the one box which they claimed contained clips marked: 
ALC, to open the case and advise us of the contents. We await tele- 
graph advice most any moment from Seattle, as to the status of this con- 
signment. In view of the foregoing, we trust you can readily appre- 
ciate the fact that we have exercised all care for the dispatch of 
these goods, and must enlighten you that if you intend to have further 
shipments to Shanghai, it would be most advisable to have same in care 
of our agent in Seattle, where individual attention may be prevalent 
as we have served you in the past for five years in New York. 


For your information, we have numerous other communicationa

the Deputy Minister of Customs at Ottawa, Canada, and should you wish 
to peruse our papers in connection with this matter if necessary, we 
shall be pleased to submit same to you. 


As soon as we hear from the Admiral Oriental Line we shall
